title: The Flying Letters of Sunny Meadow
markdown:
Once upon a time the Sunny Meadow Post Office was the neatest place in town. Stamps sat in drawers by colour and size. Packages waited in tidy piles. Every letter was a proper rectangle, address clear as day, folded just so.

Poppy, the postmaster’s niece, loved the sorting. Her fingers were quick, and her smile could chase a rainy Tuesday off a counter. Beside her perched Rune, an origami phoenix folded from paper the colours of sunset — orange, pink, and deep purple. When Rune was glad, he puffed his paper chest. His wings made a sound like dry leaves in a small breeze.

One strange Tuesday, as sun peeked over the rooftops, a letter addressed to Mrs Higgins began to wriggle. Poppy blinked. The letter stretched, grew paper wings, and fluttered up toward the high ceiling.

Before she could call her uncle, a whole stack chirped like tiny birds and swooped out the open window — a cascade of envelopes heading, quite wrongly, every which way.

“Oh no,” Poppy said, knuckles tight. Uncle Gable was out on his route. She was in charge.

Rune nudged her hand with his folded beak. The rustle was a comfort.

“We have to find them,” Poppy whispered.

A bright blue envelope zipped past and out the door, leaving a faint trail of sparkle that faded as they watched. Poppy drew a breath that still shook, and they followed.

That was the first trial: the market square, full of vendors’ shouts and the smell of new bread. A flour-dusted baker nearly tripped over a birthday card that swooped too close to his head. Poppy cupped her hands.

“Not the ovens,” she called. “The pigeonholes. Please.”

The card looped once, cheeky as a sparrow, then darted on. Rune herded two postcards away from a jam jar. Poppy’s voice felt small in the noise, but it did not stay in her throat. That counted.

The second trial was quieter. They tiptoed past Cadi, the town’s very sleepy ginger cat, who blinked one lazy eye at a letter that had become a perfect flying fish. The fish glided over Cadi’s whiskers. Cadi yawned, as if mail had always done that, and went back to being a sunbeam with fur. Poppy almost smiled. Then she saw the blue envelope waiting at the park gate, impatient as a tapping foot.

The third trial led them under the old oak that had stood for hundreds of years. Hidden among twisted roots, almost invisible against moss, was a tiny door. The blue envelope nudged it open with a paper beak.

“This way,” it rustled, which was the only sentence a letter needs when it has somewhere important to be.

Inside, a small shy creature worked among scraps. He was made entirely of crumpled paper, with big curious eyes, and it was clear he was the one giving the letters wings.

Poppy’s worry came back as a cold knot. What if he meant trouble for Uncle Gable? Rune nudged her again. She remembered her uncle’s words, said when she was unsure: even the smallest creature has a story, and sometimes a story needs a listener. She breathed, and this breath was steadier.

“Excuse me,” Poppy said, and her voice came out clear. The paper sprite jumped and dropped a letter he had been turning into a butterfly. “Why are you making all the letters fly away?”

The sprite looked at his crinkled hands. His shoulders drooped.

“I only wanted to share some joy,” he whispered. “No one notices me. I see happy letters going out, bringing smiles, and I wanted to make them more exciting. I did not mean such a muddle. I got carried away.”

Poppy’s own worry suddenly seemed a smaller thing beside his loneliness.

“It’s a good thing, wanting to share happiness,” she said. “But the letters are happy too when they arrive where they are going. That is part of the sending. Maybe you could help us put them back. Your gift could help them fly true, instead of everywhere at once.”

The sprite’s eyes lit. “Could I really?”

So the unusual team set to work. The sprite touched each changed letter with care. Poppy pointed. Rune glided. Envelopes that had been birthday cards and fish and butterflies zipped through the park, across the market, and home to the Sunny Meadow Post Office. Poppy saw each one land on the proper shelf, ready for its proper round.

By the time Uncle Gable returned, the counters were tidy. A faint sparkle still hung in the air, like a secret that had learned manners. The paper sprite bowed, no longer quite so shy, and promised to fold only the wings he was asked for. That was his making-right: to carry joy along the right addresses, not away from them.

Poppy felt warmth spread through her chest as she helped sort the mail that now stayed still. She had not let the shake in her voice keep it unsaid. Rune rustled his sunset wings in quiet agreement.

And their tale is still told whenever a letter sits square on a shelf, waiting, which is its own kind of flight. Letters are happiest when they come home to the names on their fronts.
characters: Poppy (the postmaster's niece), Rune (an origami phoenix)
